implementation_notes: Go has no destructors and no guard type, but defer is the scope-exit hook: a statement deferred right after Lock runs when the enclosing function returns, including when it panics, so `mu.Lock(); defer mu.Unlock()` is the complete realization. sync.Mutex is non-reentrant and is not tied to the data it guards, so the convention is to place the mutex field directly next to the state it protects and document the invariant. sync.RWMutex is the readers-writer form; when critical sections must be shorter than a function, put the body in a closure or a method so the defer scope matches the critical section.
pitfalls: `defer` runs at function exit, not block exit: a defer inside a loop holds every lock until the function returns; extract each iteration into a closure or method.
sync.Mutex is not reentrant - calling a method that locks the same mutex while already holding it deadlocks the goroutine.
Copying a struct that contains a sync.Mutex by value splits the lock; `go vet` warns about it, and the copy silently stops excluding the original.
A panic inside the critical section does release the mutex through defer, but the guarded data may be left inconsistent - recover or restore invariants deliberately.
